asks: A labelled diagram of an animal cell, showing the cell membrane, the cytoplasm, the nucleus, mitochondria and a small vacuole.
A labelled diagram of cheek cells as seen under a microscope, showing the cell membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus of each cell.
A labelled diagram of an animal cell beside a plant cell, showing the cell membrane, the cell wall, the nucleus, the chloroplasts and the large vacuole.
picture.why: The labelled animal cell is the drawing every learner copies into their notebook, and each part can be lit as its job is told.

big_idea.text: An animal cell is a tiny living unit: a thin membrane holds jelly-like cytoplasm, and a nucleus inside controls what the cell does.

objectives.can: Name the main parts of an animal cell and say the job of each
Explain why animal cells can take many shapes while plant cells are boxy
Predict what would go wrong if one part of a cell stopped working

why_it_matters.text: Your skin, blood and muscles are all made of cells like this, so knowing its parts is knowing how your body works.

the_why.text: A cell has to let food and oxygen in and keep its contents together, which a thin, flexible membrane does; its work happens in a liquid where things can move about, the cytoplasm; and it needs instructions to grow and divide, which the nucleus holds.

picture.text: A rounded animal cell with a soft outline. First the thin outer boundary is lit, then the jelly-like inside, then the round nucleus near the middle, then the small mitochondria and a small vacuole, each named as its job is told. Last, a plant cell appears beside it with a stiff wall, a big vacuole and green chloroplasts that the animal cell does not have.
picture.standard: labelled diagram of an animal cell

card.diagram_ask: A labelled diagram of an animal cell, showing the cell membrane, the cytoplasm, the nucleus, mitochondria and a small vacuole.

needs_first.text: All living things are made of cells.
A microscope makes very small things look big.

mistakes.mistake: Animal cells have a cell wall, like plant cells.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Animal cells have only a thin, flexible membrane; the stiff wall is found in plant cells.

mistakes.mistake: All cells have the same shape.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Animal cells have no stiff wall, so they take many shapes to suit their job: long nerve cells, round blood cells, flat skin cells.

mistakes.mistake: A cell is an empty bag with a few parts floating in it.
mistakes.why_it_fails: The inside is full of cytoplasm, a jelly in which the cell's work goes on, and each part has a job.

opening_question.question: A cell from inside your cheek and a cell from an onion are both alive. Do you think they are built the same way?
guesses: Yes, every cell is the same
No, animal cells have no parts
Mostly the same, with some differences
opening_question.answer: Mostly the same: both have a membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus, but the onion cell also has a stiff cell wall and a big vacuole.

route.what: Show a cheek cell and an onion cell side by side and ask whether they are built the same way. Ask for a guess.
Light the thin outer boundary of the animal cell. Ask: what must it let in and keep in?
Name it the cell membrane: thin, flexible, letting food and oxygen in and wastes out.
Light the jelly inside, the cytoplasm, where the cell's work happens, then the mitochondria that release energy from food.
Light the nucleus: it holds the instructions for the cell to grow and divide, so it controls the cell.
Bring the plant cell beside it: a stiff cell wall, a big vacuole and chloroplasts that the animal cell does not have.
Show cells of different shapes (nerve, blood, skin): with no stiff wall, animal cells can take any shape.
Set the task: a balloon cell with a marble nucleus.
The learner names the three main parts and says the job of each.

questions.question: Which part would you NOT find in a cell from your cheek?
questions.explain: Animal cells have a membrane and a nucleus, but no stiff cell wall.

questions.question: If a cell's membrane were torn, what would go wrong first?
options: The cytoplasm would leak out and the cell could not control what goes in and out
Nothing, because its cell wall would still hold it
Nothing, because a cell is mostly empty space
questions.explain: The membrane is what holds the cell together and lets only some things through; animal cells have no wall to fall back on.

try_it.title: A balloon cell
try_it.stands_for: The balloon is the cell membrane, the water is the cytoplasm, the marble is the nucleus and the beans are mitochondria; the box is a plant cell's wall.
try_it.predict: When you press the balloon cell gently, will it keep its shape like the box or change shape?
steps: Push the marble and the beans into the balloon.
Fill the balloon with a little water from a tap and tie it.
Press the balloon gently with your hand and watch its shape.
Put it inside the box and press the box the same way.
try_it.observe: The balloon changes shape easily and springs back, with the marble moving about inside; inside the box it keeps the box's shape.
try_it.question: Why can animal cells take so many shapes while plant cells stay boxy?
try_it.expected: Because an animal cell has only a thin, flexible membrane, like the balloon, while a plant cell also has a stiff cell wall, like the box, that holds its shape.
try_it.write: An animal cell has a thin membrane, jelly-like cytoplasm and a nucleus. It has no cell wall, so it can change shape.
try_it.in_class: Groups of four, one balloon cell per group. The teacher draws the animal cell on the board and asks groups to say which object stands for each part. Ask: what does the box stand for, and which cell has one? A group that puts the box on the animal cell still thinks all cells have walls.
